items.title: Scaffolding company fined after trainee scaffolder killed in five-metre fall
items.summary: Trainee scaffolder died after falling five metres from a partially erected scaffold while working on a housing development in North Yorkshire. HSE found the company had failed to ensure scaffolding work was carried out safely and in accordance with industry guidance. The investigation found that safe zones had not been established and workers were not […]
items.body:
- Trainee scaffolder died after falling five metres from a partially erected scaffold while working on a housing development in North Yorkshire.
- HSE found the company had failed to ensure scaffolding work was carried out safely and in accordance with industry guidance.
- The investigation found that safe zones had not been established and workers were not using harnesses or lanyards.
A scaffolding company has been fined after a trainee scaffolder died in a five-metre fall from a partially erected scaffold.
On 5 July 2023, Michael Swales was working for Ask Scaffolding Ltd, which had been contracted to provide scaffolding services for a residential housing development near Ripon in North Yorkshire.
Mr Swales and a colleague were erecting scaffolding at the front of a two-storey house under construction when he fell five metres after standing on an unsecured scaffolding board. There were inadequate measures in place to prevent or mitigate the risk of a fall. Emergency services attended, but Mr Swales died at the scene.
An investigation by the Health and Safety Executive (HSE) found that Ask Scaffolding Ltd had failed to ensure work at height was carried out in a safe manner, so far as was reasonably practicable.
The investigation found that the scaffolding work being carried out on the day of the accident was unsafe and did not follow industry guidance. Safe zones had not been established, and neither Mr Swales nor his colleague was using a harness or lanyard while working.
The investigation also found that previous scaffolding work had not been carried out in accordance with the guidance. A post-accident inspection identified that guardrails had not been installed where they should have been. Several witnesses also indicated that scaffolding work was regularly carried out by company operatives without following the guidance.
The guidance identifies the use of collective protection measures to create a ‘Scaffolder’s Safe Zone’ as the primary means of preventing falls. Personal protection, such as a harness and lanyard, should be used when a scaffolder is working without a safe zone.
All scaffolding must be erected, dismantled and altered safely. Guidance on the measures employers and scaffolding contractors should take to ensure scaffolding work is carried out safely can be found here: Scaffolds – HSE.
Ask Scaffolding Ltd, of Thornton Road Industrial Estate, Pickering, YO18 7JB, pleaded guilty to breaching Regulation 4(1)(c) of the Work at Height Regulations 2005. The company was fined £16,000 and ordered to pay £8,000 in costs and a £2,000 victim surcharge at Leeds Magistrates’ Court on 4 November 2026.
HSE Inspector David Beaton said:
“This tragic accident underlines the importance of those in control of scaffolding work making sure that it is being done safely and in accordance with industry guidance, and the potential consequences where this is not done.
“Our thoughts remain with Michael’s family and friends.”
This HSE prosecution was brought by HSE enforcement lawyer Iain Jordan and paralegal officer Zara Salman.
Further information:
- The Health and Safety Executive (HSE) is Britain’s national regulator for workplace health and safety. We are dedicated to protecting people and places, and helping everyone lead safer and healthier lives.
- More information about the legislation referred to in this case is available.
- Further details on the latest HSE news releases are available.
- Guidance on scaffolding can be found on the HSE website.
- HSE does not pass sentences, set guidelines or collect any fines imposed. items.title: Napkins manufacturer fined after worker’s hand trapped in machinery
items.summary: Worker’s right hand trapped between the print rollers of machinery The woman had worked as a machinery operator for 11 years HSE investigation found that the company failed to prevent access to dangerous parts of machinery A manufacturer of napkins and other thin ply paper products has been fined after a worker’s hand became trapped […]
items.body:
- Worker’s right hand trapped between the print rollers of machinery
- The woman had worked as a machinery operator for 11 years
- HSE investigation found that the company failed to prevent access to dangerous parts of machinery
A manufacturer of napkins and other thin ply paper products has been fined after a worker’s hand became trapped in machinery at its site in St Helens.
The experienced worker, who had been a machine operator for 11 years was cleaning the rollers of a machine that is used to emboss logos and emblems onto tissue paper before folding the napkins into shape. As she was doing this, her right hand was drawn into the machine and was trapped for several minutes.
She sustained serious injuries to her right hand including full amputations to her little finger and ring finger and partial amputations to her index and middle finger. She also has increased sensitivity in the hand. She is unable to manage daily tasks such as cooking and cannot take part in her hobbies such as cycling, knitting, and gardening due to the injury being on her dominant hand.
An investigation by the HSE found that the machine did not have an interlocked guard to prevent access to the print rollers. Therefore the dangerous moving parts of the machine could be accessed by any employee while the machine was operating. In addition to this, the company had previously been served with enforcement for other machinery guarding issues during site inspections in 2021, 2019, 2014, and 2010.
HSE guidance states employers must take effective measures to prevent access to dangerous parts of machinery. This will normally be fixed or interlocked guards which prevent persons coming into contact with those parts; this was the expected control in this instance. Further guidance can be found here Provision and Use of Work Equipment Regulations 1998 (PUWER) – HSE.
Duni Poppies Limited of Cornwall Street, St Helens pleaded guilty to breaching The Provision and Use of Work Equipment Regulations 1998, Regulation 11(1). The company was fined £80,000 and order to pay £4,756 in costs at Warrington Magistrates Court on 3 November 2026.
HSE inspector Gemma Feerick said:
“This avoidable incident led to an experienced employee suffering life changing injuries.
“If the company had properly assessing the risks and applied the correct control measures to prevent access to dangerous parts of machinery, it would have been avoided.
“We will not hesitate to take action against companies who fall below the expected standards and fail to keep people safe.”
This HSE prosecution was brought by HSE enforcement lawyer Julian White and paralegal officer Ella Loveday.
Further information:

items.title: Construction and landscaping company fined after worker falls through fragile barn roof
items.summary: • AJ Riley Landscapes and Building Limited were fined £20,000 • The worker suffered fractures to his ribs, vertebrae and pelvis after falling approximately 10 metres • Falls from height remain one of the leading causes of workplace fatalities A Lancashire based construction and landscaping company has been fined £20,000 after a worker suffered serious […]
items.body:
• AJ Riley Landscapes and Building Limited were fined £20,000
• The worker suffered fractures to his ribs, vertebrae and pelvis after falling approximately 10 metres
• Falls from height remain one of the leading causes of workplace fatalities
A Lancashire based construction and landscaping company has been fined £20,000 after a worker suffered serious injuries when he fell through the fragile roof of a barn.
Josh Huddleston, 47, who was employed by AJ Riley Landscapes and Building Limited, was replacing a damaged skylight on the roof of the barn when the incident occurred on 24th February 2025. He suffered fractures to his ribs, vertebrae and pelvis after falling approximately 10 metres.
An investigation by the Health and Safety Executive (HSE) found that AJ Riley Landscapes and Building Limited had failed to adequately plan the work and ensure appropriate control measures were in place to prevent Mr Huddleston from falling through the fragile roof.
The investigation also found that workers had not received sufficient training to ensure they were competent in the use of the control measures identified in the company’s risk assessment.
HSE guidance states that employers must ensure work at height is properly planned, appropriately supervised and carried out by competent people. Where work at height is necessary, employers must take suitable and sufficient measures to prevent, so far as is reasonably practicable, anyone falling a distance liable to cause personal injury.
Work on fragile roofs presents significant risks and employers and contractors must ensure appropriate precautions are in place before work begins. HSE’s guidance on working on roofs provides further information on managing these risks.
AJ Riley Landscapes and Building Limited, of Caton, Lancashire, pleaded guilty to breaching Section 2(1) of the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974. The company was fined £20,000 and ordered to pay £4,955 in costs at Warrington Magistrates’ Court on 3 November 2026.
Following the hearing, HSE inspector Matthew Shepherd said:
“Falls from height remain one of the leading causes of workplace fatalities. It is fortunate that Mr Huddleston survived this fall, which could easily have resulted in fatal injuries.
“The risks associated with working at height on fragile roof surfaces are well known. AJ Riley Landscapes and Building Limited failed to ensure appropriate control measures were in place to prevent a worker falling through the roof.
“Suitable precautions are readily available, and this incident could have been prevented through proper planning, risk assessment and the implementation of effective control measures.
“This prosecution should serve as a reminder to all employers and contractors undertaking work at height that they have a duty to protect their workers. HSE will not hesitate to take enforcement action against those who fail to meet their legal responsibilities.”
The prosecution was brought by HSE enforcement lawyer Gemma Zakrzewski and paralegal officer Henrietta Burrows.

items.title: “He had his whole life ahead of him”; Company fined after 21-year-old tyre fitter killed when truck fell on him at roadside
items.summary: Niall Fawcett died when he was struck by a truck while he was working beneath it on the M56 slip road in Cheshire. HSE found the company failed to properly assess risks of replacing a blown-out tyre on a low-profile truck. Victim was not adequately supervised or monitored despite only holding roadside licence for less […]
items.body:
- Niall Fawcett died when he was struck by a truck while he was working beneath it on the M56 slip road in Cheshire.
- HSE found the company failed to properly assess risks of replacing a blown-out tyre on a low-profile truck.
- Victim was not adequately supervised or monitored despite only holding roadside licence for less than four months.
A commercial tyre service provider in Worcestershire has been fined following the death of 21-year-old employee Niall Fawcett, who was killed while carrying out a roadside repair.
On 2 August 2024, Mr Fawcett was called out to replace a blown-out tyre on a low-profile truck on the slip road at junction 7 of the M56 motorway near Bowdon. While he was positioned beneath the truck, it is understood to have slipped from the bottle jack (a compact hydraulic lifting tool designed for vehicle support) being used to raise the vehicle and landed on him, causing fatal head injuries.
An investigation by the Health and Safety Executive (HSE) found that Halford Commercial Fleet Services Limited, formerly known as Lodge Tyre Company Limited (The), had not properly assessed the risks associated with replacing a blown-out tyre on a low-profile vehicle. The company had also failed to give employees suitable work instructions, including information on when a truck should be recovered rather than repaired at the roadside.
The investigation also found that Mr Fawcett had only obtained his licence to work on commercial tyres at the roadside when he joined the company less than four months before his death. Despite this, he had not been subject to any monitoring or supervision to ensure that he was working safely.
The HSE publication Health and safety in motor vehicle repair and associated industries sets out the importance of providing safe systems of work and ensuring workers are competent to carry out their tasks.
The impact on Niall’s family
Niall’s mother, Sharon, said in her victim personal statement:
“Niall was only 21 years old when he died. He had his whole life ahead of him. He was planning to marry the following year and he and Megan were saving for a deposit on their first home together and talking about starting a family. Niall was building for a life he was excited for and this was taken from him in an instant.
“Niall went to work that day and should have been safe, supported and protected. Instead, my son never came home.”
Halford Commercial Fleet Services Limited, of Icknield Street Drive, Washford West, Redditch, Worcestershire B98 0DE, pleaded guilty to breaching Section 2(1) of the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974. The company was fined £600,000 and ordered to pay a victim surcharge of £200 and £24,203 in costs at Warrington Magistrates’ Court on 3 November 2026.
HSE Principal Inspector Laura Royales said:
“This case should serve to highlight to employers the importance of properly assessing the risks to which their workers are exposed and providing the right information and instructions, supplemented by adequate monitoring and supervision arrangements, to ensure that they can and do work safely.
Our thoughts remain with Niall’s family as they continue to come to terms with their tragic loss.”
This HSE prosecution was brought by HSE enforcement lawyer Matthew Reynolds and paralegal officer Benjamin Stobbart. The investigation was supported by Visiting Officer Natty Heath.
Further information:
- The Health and Safety Executive (HSE) is Britain’s national regulator for workplace health and safety. We are dedicated to protecting people and places, and helping everyone lead safer and healthier lives.
- More information about the legislation referred to in this case is available.
- Further details on the latest HSE news releases is available.
- Relevant guidance can be found here Health and safety in motor vehicle repair and associated industries
- HSE does not pass sentences, set guidelines or collect any fines imposed. Relevant sentencing guidelines must be followed unless the court is satisfied that it would be contrary to the interests of justice to do so. The sentencing guidelines for health and safety offences can be found here.

items.title: PICTURED: Aftermath of apartment roof blaze workers ‘lucky to escape’ from
items.summary: Photos taken after fire on roof of apartment block show damage Four workers forced to flee blaze with just one ladder as their escape route No fire extinguishers, no means of raising the alarm and no permit for welding work C Watkins Plumbing Limited fined after HSE investigation finds company failed to follow its own […]
items.body:
- Photos taken after fire on roof of apartment block show damage
- Four workers forced to flee blaze with just one ladder as their escape route
- No fire extinguishers, no means of raising the alarm and no permit for welding work
- C Watkins Plumbing Limited fined after HSE investigation finds company failed to follow its own hot works procedures
Shocking photographs taken in the aftermath of a fire on the roof of an apartment block in Surrey show how lucky four workers were to escape.
A contractor has been fined after the workers had to flee a fire that engulfed the roof of a 14-storey apartment building under construction in Surrey.
The four subcontractors were working under the control of C Watkins Plumbing Limited, installing an air source heat pump on the roof of the Old Telephone Exchange development in Staines-upon-Thames, when the incident happened on 26 July 2024.
Sparks from welding work ignited uncovered rigid foam insulation that had been laid across the roof. The self-sustaining fire developed quickly, spreading across the whole of the roof space before burning itself out when it ran out of fuel.
The men escaped through a single opening in the floor and down a ladder to Level 14. There was no other way off the roof, no means of raising the alarm, and no fire extinguishers.
An investigation by the Health and Safety Executive (HSE) found that the company had failed to plan, manage and monitor the hot works on the roof. Despite the company having policies requiring them, there was no risk assessment or method statement in place, and a permit to work was not issued for the welding.
HSE’s guidance, HSG168 – Fire Safety in Construction, states that fire safety measures must be considered throughout all stages of design and procurement, and implemented effectively during construction. It says risk assessments must identify high-risk activities where fires can spread quickly, and situations where evacuation plans are complex, and that all risk assessments and control measures must be reviewed throughout the construction phase to make sure they remain suitable and sufficient.
C Watkins Plumbing Limited, of Watkins House, Leigh Road, Haine Industrial Park, Ramsgate, Kent, pleaded guilty to breaching Regulation 15(2) of the Construction (Design and Management) Regulations 2015. The company was fined £20,000 and ordered to pay £8,270 in costs at Staines Magistrates’ Court on 29 October 2026.
HSE inspector Stephanie Hickford-Smith said:
“Watkins failed to follow its own procedures for hot works. It did not assess the risks and so had no control measures in place.
“The four men working on the roof were lucky to escape. Had the fire started closer to their escape route, or had they not acted as quickly as they did, the outcome could have been devastatingly different.”
This HSE prosecution was brought by HSE senior enforcement lawyers James Towey and Laura Lax and paralegal officer Farhat Basir.
Further information:
- The Health and Safety Executive (HSE) is Britain’s national regulator for workplace health and safety. We are dedicated to protecting people and places, and helping everyone lead safer and healthier lives.
- More information about the legislation referred to in this case is available.
- Further details on the latest HSE news releases is available.
- HSE does not pass sentences, set guidelines or collect any fines imposed. items.title: “This accident took away my freedom”; Vehicle recovery company fined after worker crushed under truck left unable to walk unaided
items.summary: Simon Pedder was crushed under a reversing recovery truck and now needs crutches, a frame and a wheelchair. More than 10 months on, he has been unable to return to work and says, “life will never be the same”. HSE found the company had no suitable traffic management system and no adequate precautions for reversing […]
items.body:
- Simon Pedder was crushed under a reversing recovery truck and now needs crutches, a frame and a wheelchair.
- More than 10 months on, he has been unable to return to work and says, “life will never be the same”.
- HSE found the company had no suitable traffic management system and no adequate precautions for reversing vehicles – which remain a leading cause of workplace injury.
A Swindon-based vehicle recovery business has been fined after a worker was struck by a reversing vehicle and suffered life-changing injuries.
On 13 June 2025, Simon Pedder was undertaking yard duties at Cotswold Vehicle Recovery (Swindon) Limited in Highworth when he was suddenly hit and crushed under a company-owned recovery truck.
Mr Pedder suffered fractures to both legs and an arm, a punctured lung and a fractured rib. He was airlifted to the John Radcliffe Hospital in Oxford, where he spent five weeks and underwent several operations to rebuild his legs, including skin grafts.
An investigation by the Health and Safety Executive (HSE) found that Cotswold Vehicle Recovery (Swindon) Limited had failed to implement a suitable traffic management system to make sure vehicles and pedestrians could circulate safely and had not implemented proper precautions to assist reversing drivers.
(Photographs showing before and after HSE intervention)
More than 10 months later, Mr Pedder’s recovery has not progressed as he had hoped. The extent of his injuries means that in addition to using crutches, a Zimmer frame and wheelchair, Simon now needs regular care visits and cannot carry out basic tasks like getting into the shower without help. He has been told he will most likely need walking aids for the rest of his life.
Describing the impact of the incident on his life, Mr Pedder said:
“I used to be a very sociable person, the life of the party, both in work and with friends; this has been taken away from me as now I spend my days sitting at home by myself. My mood is very low, and this is affecting not only myself but also my family, who say my personality appears to have changed completely.”
He added, “there are many basic things I can’t do, for example, I can’t cut the grass, I can’t fold the washing, I can’t go for a walk, and I am not allowed to drive. This accident took away my freedom.”
He also described the impact on his family, with his wife cutting short her working hours to support his care, and the family rearranging the living room to accommodate a hospital bed. Mr Pedder said: “I feel so bad because I am affecting those who are close to me. My life will never be the same and I feel like this accident should never have happened as I was only doing my job.”
Failure to manage reversing vehicle risks
HSE inspectors found failures by Cotswold Vehicle Recovery (Swindon) Limited to properly control the risk of reversing vehicles – despite this being one of the leading causes of workplace fatal injury. To manage workplace transport effectively, employers should consider the risks associated with their site and vehicles. Where workers are required to operate on foot in areas where there are moving vehicles, employers must ensure traffic routes are organised in a way that prevents collisions between pedestrians and vehicles.
HSE guidance advises implementing a one-way system for vehicle circulation to eliminate the need for reversing. Where this isn’t possible, the site should be organised to include safety measures such as protective barriers, clear markings and pedestrian crossing points. To aid a driver’s field of vision and alert pedestrians to reversing vehicles, precautionary measures such as rear-view cameras and warning alarms should also be fitted to vehicles.
Guidance on workplace transport safety is freely available on the HSE website: Workplace transport – HSE.
Cotswold Vehicle Recovery (Swindon) Limited, based at Blackworth Industrial Estate, Highworth, pleaded guilty to breaching Section 2(1) of the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974. The company was fined £28,000 and ordered to pay £2,000 in costs at Bristol Magistrates’ Court on 29 October 2026.
HSE Inspector Laura Artosi said:
“Almost 25 per cent of fatal workplace transport accidents in Great Britain occur while a vehicle is reversing – a stark reminder to employers to properly assess and manage this fundamental risk.
“Cotswold Vehicle Recovery (Swindon) Limited lacked a suitable traffic management system, including adequate arrangements to ensure vehicles could reverse without risks to those on foot. These failings led to an incident that has robbed Simon Pedder of much of his freedom and will likely have a lasting impact on his life.
“Had Cotswold Vehicle Recovery (Swindon) Limited implemented robust measures to allow pedestrians and vehicles to move safely across its site, this incident would not have occurred.”
This HSE prosecution was brought by HSE enforcement lawyer Karen Park and paralegal officer Michael Millman.

items.title: Fish processing firm fined almost a quarter of a million pounds after worker’s arm pulled into machine after safety guard left off
items.summary: Worker suffered fractured jaw and chest and arm trauma when he was pulled into a conveyor mechanism A section of fixed guarding had been removed two weeks earlier and not replaced Company’s guarding checks did not include non-electrical fixed guards A Peterhead fish processing company has been fined £245,000 after a worker was dragged into […]
items.body:
- Worker suffered fractured jaw and chest and arm trauma when he was pulled into a conveyor mechanism
- A section of fixed guarding had been removed two weeks earlier and not replaced
- Company’s guarding checks did not include non-electrical fixed guards
A Peterhead fish processing company has been fined £245,000 after a worker was dragged into a machine through a gap where a safety guard should have been.
The man, then aged 30, was working as a chargehand on a production line at Lunar Freezing and Cold Storage Company Limited’s premises in Peterhead on 19 August 2025 when the incident happened.
What happened
The worker had stopped to deal with a box that had jammed too high in a rack loader cage to be reached from the ground. He entered the production line through a gap in the guarding without isolating the power, then climbed onto the conveyor and pressed down on the lid to release the jam. The machine restarted, and his right arm was pulled into the pusher section of the rack loader. Unable to free himself, he was drawn further into the mechanism until his head made contact with moving parts.
A colleague who heard the worker’s shouts for help isolated the power and stopped the machine. The man was taken to Aberdeen Royal Infirmary, where he was found to have a fractured jaw and trauma to his chest and right arm. He needed surgery to insert metal plates in his jaw and spent three days in hospital. He returned to work on 29 September 2025 and has made a full recovery.
HSE investigation
An investigation by the Health and Safety Executive (HSE) found that a section of fixed guarding next to the production line had been removed during maintenance around two weeks before the incident and had not been put back. Without the guard, the gap gave access to the machine without the power being isolated. The correct route in, through an interlocked gate, would have switched off the machinery as soon as the gate was opened.
HSE found that, while the guard was missing, staff had used the gap to reach the machinery on various occasions when boxes jammed, rather than the interlocked gate. Maintenance staff told HSE they had seen the guard missing and had seen employees using the gap, but it was not reinstated. The weekly inspection checklist used by the in-house maintenance team did not include checking the integrity of non-electrical fixed guarding.
Had the guarding been in place, the only way into the machine would have been through the interlocked gate, and the incident would not have happened.
HSE guidance highlights the importance of following safe isolation and lock-off procedures before any maintenance or cleaning work is carried out. Employers must ensure all machinery is properly isolated from power sources, and that systems are regularly monitored and reviewed to prevent inadvertent start-up. Further guidance is available here: The safe isolation of plant and equipment – HSE.
Lunar Freezing and Cold Storage Company Ltd, of East Quay, The Harbour, Peterhead, pleaded guilty to breaching Regulation 11(1) and (2) of the Provision and Use of Work Equipment Regulations 1998 and Section 33(1)(c) of the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974. The company was fined £245,000 and ordered to pay a with a victim surcharge of £18,375, at Peterhead Sheriff Court on 28 October 2026.
HSE inspector Nicky Smith said:
“This was a wholly preventable incident which left a worker seriously injured.
“A missing guard and an unchecked gap left the way open for a worker to be dragged into a machine.
“Guards must be kept in place, and checks must cover every guard, not just the electrical ones.”

items.title: Engineering company fined after worker suffers finger amputation
items.summary: Worker suffered a partial finger amputation when he reached into an inadequately guarded saw. HSE investigation found the company had failed to take effective measures to prevent access to dangerous moving parts. Company fined after pleading guilty to breaching PUWER 1998. An engineering company has been fined £20,000 and ordered to pay £15,000 in compensation […]
items.body:
- Worker suffered a partial finger amputation when he reached into an inadequately guarded saw.
- HSE investigation found the company had failed to take effective measures to prevent access to dangerous moving parts.
- Company fined after pleading guilty to breaching PUWER 1998.
An engineering company has been fined £20,000 and ordered to pay £15,000 in compensation after a worker suffered a partial finger amputation when he reached into an inadequately guarded automatic saw.
Thomas Davies, 21, was working for Dlinexsign Ltd when the incident occurred. Having reached into the machine to retrieve a cut piece of material, his hand came into contact with the moving saw blade, resulting in him losing part of his finger.
The incident occurred at the company’s premises at Buckingham Road Industrial Estate, Brackley. The machine was used to cut lengths of material, and Mr Davies was able to reach into the machine and access the dangerous moving parts while it was operating.
An investigation by the Health and Safety Executive (HSE) found that Dlinexsign Ltd had failed to take effective measures to prevent access to the dangerous parts of the machinery.
HSE guidance states that employers must take effective measures to prevent access to dangerous parts of machinery. This will normally be achieved using fixed guarding, but where access is required, other protective measures such as interlocked guards may be necessary to ensure dangerous movement has stopped before a person can reach the danger zone.
Further guidance can be found on HSE’s website on the safe use of work equipment: Introduction to machinery safety – HSE.
Dlinexsign Ltd, of Shires Road, Brackley, pleaded guilty to breaching Regulation 11(1) of the Provision and Use of Work Equipment Regulations 1998. The company was fined £20,000 and ordered to pay £15,000 in compensation to Mr Davies, and £9,064.34 in prosecution costs at Milton Keynes Magistrates’ Court on 23 October 2026.
HSE Inspector Dulanjala Kandana-Arachchige said:
“This incident demonstrates the serious consequences that can result when access to dangerous parts of machinery is not effectively prevented.
“Employers must ensure that machinery is properly guarded and that effective measures are in place to prevent workers from reaching dangerous moving parts.
“This was a preventable incident. Employers have a responsibility to ensure that work equipment can be used safely and that workers are protected from dangerous machinery.”
This HSE prosecution was brought by HSE enforcement lawyer Tom Ledden-Rocks and paralegal officer Natalie Ellis.
Further information:
- The Health and Safety Executive (HSE) is Britain’s national regulator for workplace health and safety. We are dedicated to protecting people and places and helping everyone lead safer and healthier lives.
- More information about the legislation referred to in this case is available.
- Further details on the latest HSE news releases is available.
- Guidance on machinery safety can be found here: Introduction to machinery safety – HSE
- HSE does not pass sentences, set guidelines or collect any fines imposed. Relevant sentencing guidelines must be followed unless the court is satisfied that it would be contrary to the interests of justice to do so. The sentencing guidelines for health and safety offences in England can be found here and those for Scotland here.
